ORIGINAL ARTICLE
The effect of clinical pilates‑based physiotherapy program for a Stiff 
Person Syndrome patient: a case report
Beliz Belgen Kaygisiz1  · Fahriye Çoban1  · Ferda Selcuk2 
Received: 17 June 2020 / Accepted: 15 September 2020 / Published online: 30 September 2020 
© Belgian Neurological Society 2020
Abstract
The aim of the present report is to show the effects of a clinical pilates-based physiotherapy training program on physical 
functioning, including balance ability, flexibility, muscle strength, and pain severity in a case with Stiff Person Syndrome 
(SPS). A 43-year-old female with a 3-year history of SPS participated in the study. Clinical pilates training exercises were 
performed two times per week during 8 weeks. Static balance was evaluated with One Leg Stance Test and Tandem Stance 
Test, dynamic balance with Functional Reach Test and lower extremity strength and endurance measured by 30-s Chair Stand 
Test. Berg Balance Scale was used to assess balance and fall risk, and Timed Up and Go Test was used to assess functional 
mobility. Pain evaluation was done by Pain Quality Assessment Scale. Flexibility was measured with tape measure, range 
of motion with goniometer and muscle strength with manual muscle test. Among the balance and functional mobility tests, 
progress has been observed in all tests, except for 30-s Chair Stand test. Improvements have been observed in patient’s range 
of motion, flexibility, strength, pain and balance parameters. Clinical pilates-based physiotherapy program had positive 
effects on many physical and functional parameters of the patient and can be used as a safe exercise method in physiotherapy 
rehabilitation of SPS.
Keywords Stiff Person Syndrome · Physiotherapy · Pilates training
Introduction
“Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS)”, first reported by Moerch and 
Woltman in 1956 [1], is a rare neurological disease charac-
terized by stiffness and painful muscle spasms primarily in 
the abdominal, axial and extremity muscles [1 ]. The exact 
prevalence of SPS is uncertain, but the incidence is esti-
mated to be approximately 1 in one million people between 
both sexes, but predominantly female [2].
Stiffness is the most common symptom and is often one 
of the first symptoms to notice and it causes pain frequently 
[2]. Later in disease, it is reported that 65% of patients can-
not perform normal activities in daily life due to stiffness, 
rigidity, unpredictable spasms and/or frequent falls [3 ]. 
When spasms affect the paraspinal muscles, the resulting 
hyperextension can sometimes be severe enough to lift a 
person from the chair [4]. Also, pain as another symptom, is 
common in SPS. It is typically chronic but worsens acutely 
with muscle spasms. Therefore, pain affects quality of life of 
patients negatively [5]. Patients are reported to have abdomi-
nal muscles "like wood" and there is a difficulty leaning 
forward [6]. Walking is often wide, cautious and slow as the 
person makes efforts to maintain balance and prevent falls 
[3]. Also, patients with SPS may walk as if their legs are stiff 
like a "tin man" due to the excessive stiffness in the lower 
extremity muscles [6]. Falls are seen quite frequently due to 
severe spasms. Sometimes, fear of falling can force patients 
to use walking aids (walking stick or wheelchair) even if the

severity of rigidity does not make this necessary [7 ].
Physiotherapy training is substantiated to be a necessary 
and beneficial intervention in rehabilitation of patients

with SPS [6 , 8–10]. The effect of different physiotherapy 
interventions on SPS management has been studied. Inter -
vention models such as stretching exercises [4 , 11–14], 
strengthening exercises [13, 14], massages [4 ], relaxation 
exercises [11, 12], range of motion exercises (ROM) [12, 
13], postural exercises [14], ultrasound [4 ], and hydro-
therapy [6 ] are used. Lorish et al. presented one of the 
first articles describing the benefits of physiotherapy in the 
treatment of SPS [6 ]. Later studies have also shown that 
stretching and postural exercises reduce excessive lum-
bar lordosis and pain [9 , 10]. The cross-friction massage 
applied to tendons has been found to reduce muscle stiff-
ness and control painful spasm in the muscles [4 ]. In the 
same study, ultrasound therapy was used to reduce muscle 
spasm and joint stiffness [4 ]. However, as far as we know, 
clinical Pilates (CP) training which has been widespread 
and high in evidence in the rehabilitation of neurologically 
affected patients in recent years has not been used as a 
therapeutic intervention in SPS.
Pilates was created by Joseph Pilates in 1920 and Austral-
ian physiotherapists gathered this method under the name of 
Modified (Clinical) Pilates exercises and made them suitable 
for the clinic [15]. CP exercises are defined as an exercise 
model that increases and protects muscular endurance, flex-
ibility and muscle strength [16]. The aim of this exercise 
model is to increase the awareness of the neutral position 
of the spine and to strengthen the deep postural muscles 
of the spine. During exercises, training of the muscles of 
the trunk is focused, and the body stabilization is achieved, 
and more difficult activities are initiated, thereby improving 
body awareness [15]. With these studies for the spine, it is 
also aimed to increase balance and stability [17]. There are 
some general principles that must be followed during CP 
exercises. These are: concentration, breathing, focusing in 
the center, control, stability and isolation. These principles 
are provided by the simultaneous muscle activations of the 
muscles responsible for trunk stabilization (multifidus, dia-
phragm, transversus abdominis and pelvic floor muscles) 
[17]. There is evidence that pilates is an effective form of 
exercise for patients with multiple sclerosis, a neurological 
disorder that affects motor and non-motor function.[18]. In a 
recent review, methods such as massage, ultrasound, hydro-
therapy, relaxation, stretching and posture exercises, but no 
CP training were discussed in SPS population.[8 ].
Randomized controlled trials are not possible to conduct 
in SPS patient populations, as it has a low incidence. In the 
literature, treatment-related studies have been carried out in 
the form of case reports/case series. CP exercises have been 
shown to have positive effects on physical and functional 
capacity in many different populations, including some 
patients with neurological diagnosis. The aim of this study is 
to show the effects of a clinical Pilates-based physiotherapy 
training program on physical functioning, including balance 
ability, flexibility, muscle strength, and pain severity in a 
case with Stiff Person Syndrome(SPS).
Case presentation
AE is a 43-year-old women (BMI: 22.9 kg/m2) who referred 
to physiotherapy center for evaluation and treatment of low

back pain and gait disturbances associated with SPS. Her 
diagnosis had been confirmed by a neurologist at a major 
state hospital. Patient is an assistant manager at a bank and 
thinks her job is stressful and she has quite a lot of respon-
sibility. She is married and has two children. She has no 
known other illness than SPS.
Disease history
The patient first applied to a neurologist with numbness and 
tingling in lower and upper extremities, as well as neck and 
low back pain and fatigue at the beginning of 2016 and diag-
nosed as Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Over time, the patient 
complained about muscle stiffness increasing gradually 
until night. She stated that she has increased difficulty in 
walking, increased muscle spasms and PD drugs did not 
work. Also, the patient had started to experience recurrent 
falls which affected her daily activities. At the beginning of 
2017, she had been re-examined thoroughly by her neurolo-
gist with blood tests, X-ray, magnetic resonance imaging 
and computed tomography scan, and high serum level of 
GAD antibodies confirmed that she has SPS. The patient 
firstly applied to a physiotherapy and rehabilitation clinic 
in a medical institution with complaints of stiffness, pain, 
balance disorder and functional limitations. However, she 
stopped treatment by saying that her mobility was not getting 
better and her motivation lost. Her doctor recommended the 
patient to try Pilates training and she started Pilates training 
for 1 year, 3 sessions per week with a personal trainer. This 
training improved her pain level, but her spasms did not 
decrease and her stiffness continued. After three months of 
ending this training, her neurologist referred her to join a CP 
training program conducted by a certified physiotherapist in 
this area. The symptoms and complaints of the patient made 
her physician and physiotherapist to think that this train-
ing method can improve physical and functional capacity of 
the patient which is shown to be effective in these types of 
physical impairments and functional limitations in patients 
with neurologic problems.
When the patient applied for CP training, she had com-
plaints about increased low back pain, balance distributions 
during the day and frequent spasms toward the end of the 
day. She also indicated that she has difficulties in leaning 
forward and wearing shoes. On examination, she showed 
signs of rigidity in lumbar region as well as in lower and

1 3
upper extremities. She had no tremor and was having trouble 
lying on bed and turning around in bed. Her medications at 
the time of evaluation include gabapentin, benzodiazepine 
and weekly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg).
Before the study, the patient was informed in detail 
about the study protocol and the informed consent form 
was signed. Medical treatment of the individual continued 
in the same way. No changes were made in the drugs recom-
mended by the neurologist during the study. The case has 
been evaluated in detail at the beginning and end of the study 
by the primary investigator (BBK).
Physiotherapy evaluation
Range of motion
Goniometric measurements were made for joints of upper 
extremity, lower extremity and vertebral column. Range of 
motion (ROM) values of the patient’s back extension, all 
movements of the hip, knee flexion–extension, ankle dorsi-
plantar flexion, all movements of the shoulder and elbow 
flexion–extension were evaluated [19].
Flexibility
Flexibility was measured with the method suggested by 
Karaduman [20]. Trunk hyperextension, trunk lateral flex-
ion, hip abduction movement flexibility and hamstring and 
quadriceps femoris muscle flexibility were measured.
Muscle strength
For muscle strength testing, manual muscle testing method 
was used. 0–5 measurements were made using standard tech-
niques described by Clarkson and Gilewich. The strength of 
patient’s lumbar extension, all movements of the shoulder, 
elbow flexion and extension, all movements of the hip, knee 
extension–flexion, ankle dorsiflexion–plantar flexion move-
ments were measured [19].
Pain
Pain severity was measured by Pain Quality Assessment 
Scale (PQAS). The PQAS asks respondents to rate the 
severity of each of 20 pain (quality and spatial) descriptor 
domains using 0–10 numeric rating scales, in which 0 indi-
cates “no pain” and 10 “the most pain sensation imagina-
ble.” With this scale, the severity of the pain was determined 
according to the type [21].
Balance
Static balance of the participants was measured by One Leg 
Stance Test (OLS) [22] and Tandem Stance Test (TST) [23] 
which are valid methods to measure the ability to balance 
and stand. These tests also gives an idea about the balance 
ability of the individual and the risk of falling. Dynamic 
balance was tested by Functional Reach Test (FRT) which 
is a reliable and valid measure [24]. The patient is asked to 
lift his arm 90° up and place it at shoulder level and to lean 
forward as far as he can on the edge of the wall without 
any loss of movement or balance in the feet. The reduced 
reach ability indicates an increased risk of falling. 30-s Chair 
Stand Test which is a reliable and valid measure used to 
assess lower extremity strength and endurance. The number 
of sitting and getting up within 30 s gives the score of the 
test [25]. Risk of falling together with static and dynamic 
balance performance was measured by Berg Balance Scale 
(BBS) which is a commonly used, reliable and valid meas-
ure. It is a 14-item test that uses sequential scoring from 0 to 
4 for each item. The total score range is between 0 and 56, 
and a higher score indicates a better balance [26].
Functional mobility
Functional mobility was evaluated with the Timed Up and 
Go Test (TUG) which is a reliable and valid test. When the 
command "Go" is given, the patient stands up from a normal

chair, walks 3 m, turns and walks back to the chair and sits. 
Time begins when commanded and ends when the person 
sits back in the chair [27].
Intervention
CP-based physiotherapy training was performed twice a 
week during 8 weeks with a certified physiotherapist (FC) 
who was blinded to assessment results. The movements of 
main exercises implemented within the scope of CP train-
ing included: Warm-up exercises (15 min): Posture exer -
cises*, Calisthenic exercises*, ROM*, Upper Extremity 
PNF patterns, Mini Squat, Spine Stretch*, Chest Stretch*. 
Main exercises (30 min): Standing balance exercises, block 
jumping, side walking, cross walking, tandem walking. Mat 
exercises: Hundreds, Shoulder Bridge, One leg stretch, Hip 
twist, Oblique Preparation, Abdominal preparation, Arm 
openings, Side Kick, Lift lower, Left Lifts, Clam Prone posi-
tion; Swan dive, One leg kick, Swimming, Cobra. Cool-
down exercises (15 min): Cat Stretch*, Spine Stretch, The 
Saw, Mermaid, Chest stretch, Swinging, Quadriceps femo-
ris stretching*, Gluteus maximus stretching*, Hamstring 
stretching*, Hip flexor stretching* and end of the cool-down 
exercise, relaxation training* is applied such as: positioning

1 3
supine, supported by pillows. Along with positioning, res-
piratory control consisted of breathing exercises. In addition, 
a home program was given to the patient, which consisted 
of * exercises, to do 1 h per day (for the days when she does 
not join to program) and it has been checked every session.
Results
Table  1 shows the results of balance and functional mobility 
tests and flexibility measurements. Among the balance and 
functional mobility tests, progress has been observed in all 
tests, except for 30-s Chair Stand test. In addition, improve-
ments were seen in all of the flexibility measurements.
Manual muscle test and ROM measurements are shown 
in Table  2. According to manual muscle testing, all muscle 
strength scores improved, except ankle dorsiflexion, shoul-
der internal–external rotation and elbow extension scores, 
bilaterally. In addition, according to ROM measurements, all 
ranges increased except hip flexion of the left side, adduc-
tion of the both side, internal rotation of the right side, ankle 
dorsiflexion of the left and shoulder abduction of the right 
side values.
Table  3 shows comparison of PQAS before and after 
treatment. It was observed that the total score of the scale 
decreased from 120 to 89. Especially in 10 items, there was 
an improvement: pain intensity, stinging pain, burning, 
crushing sensation, striking-type pain, numbness, tingling, 
spasm, spreading and feeling of heaviness. The biggest dif-
ference after treatment was seen in the spasm subscale. The 
patient stated the spasm score as 9/10 before the treatment, 
and 5/10 after the treatment. Apart from this, there was an 
improvement in stinging and burning pain. While the patient 
gave 9/10 for the sinking and burning-type pain points before 
the treatment, it was reported as 6/10 after the treatment.
Discussion
This case report describes the CP training for a patient with 
Stiff Person Syndrome. CP exercises focus specifically on 
strengthening deep postural muscles of the spine providing 
trunk stabilization due to the principles it contains; in addi-
tion, has been shown to improve flexibility and pain level. 
Due to these effects, this method was preferred to be used 
as an intervention for a SPS patient who presented stiffness 
and painful spasms in the trunk and lower extremities. Our 
case showed improvements in most of the outcome measures 
with different levels.
Most devastating symptom of our patient was pain which 
was not distorted as pain and painful muscle spasm is among 
the most prominent symptoms of Stiff Person Syndrome [7]. 
In a study done by Kahraman et al., balance and coordination 
exercises, posture, strengthening, functional mobility exer -
cises and stretching exercises were not effective on pain [14]. 
However, in a recent systematic review done by Vaiyapuri 
et al., where nine case report studies have been reviewed, 
authors stated that physiotherapy and rehabilitation inter -
ventions including massage, electrotherapeutic modalities, 
hydrotherapy, relaxation, and stretching exercises resulted 
in a significant decrease in pain, spasm and stiffness [8 ]. 
The result of our study is parallel to many studies covered 
with this review. Among the pain quality assessments, the 
’cramping’ sub-dimension decreased from 9 to 5 points and 
was the most improved complaint. Literature shows that 
physical modalities such as heat, ice, massage, and range

of motion exercises, soft tissue mobilization, stretching and 
relaxation exercises can suppress local spasm and prevent 
contractures [4, 11, 12]. Additionally, in Parkinson’s disease 
patients, which is a neurologic group of patients with simi-
lar symptoms, an 8-week Pilates training was applied and 
complaints such as pain and cramps were reduced [28]. The 
approach that we applied in our study consisted of stretch-
ing and relaxation components. So, we can say that the

stretching and relaxation exercises included in our training 
method have decreased the level of pain and spasms.
Karaoglan et al. [13] showed benefits of abdominal 
strengthening exercises in improving gait and trunk move-
ments in a SPS case. ROM, stretching and strengthening 
exercises were prescribed for abdominal muscles and follow-
up assessments were done after 3 weeks [13]. The method 
used in our study also has strengthening components, but 
dumbbells, weights or therabands are not used and this 
method have been shown to increase core endurance and 
provide trunk stabilization and also, in turn, helps to achieve 
improvement walking capacity and functional mobility [28]. 
The results of our study is parallel to the study done by 
Karaoglan. Also, it is suggested that strengthening exercises 
should be included in the program to prevent the develop-
ment of long-term disability for the SPS patients [8 ].
Reduced flexibility and ROM in SPS should be avoided 
as it may cause contractures, deformities and impaired func-
tional mobility [8 ]. In a case study done by Poter K.[11], 
the patient received therapeutic exercises and functional 
retraining for 30 min, 3 sessions a week for 10 days. Conse-
quently, the patient showed improvements in ROM, posture, 
and gait [11]. In a meta-analysis examining CP in healthy 
individuals, they have demonstrated strong evidence that CP 
increases flexibility [29]. As a neurological patient group, 
CP exercises was applied in Parkinson’s disease and it was 
found that the flexibility of the lower limbs increased [30].

Our results are parallel to literature and were expected as 
CP includes components of ROM and relaxation exercises.
In the field of Stiff Person Syndrome, more studies on 
spasm and pain have been conducted to date. Although 
the training model used focuses on the center of the body 
and many studies in neurologic population have showed 
that it improves balance [18, 31], balance assessment and 
training studies in SPS population are limited in the liter -
ature. In the case report by Kahraman et al. [14], patient 
has received exercises for balance, coordination, posture, 
strength and flexibility and authors revealed that the patient 
had improved balance and gait. In a systematic review exam-
ining the effects of Pilates training in Parkinson’s disease 
which has similar symptoms to SPS, Pilates has been found 
to provide a significant improvement on balance [31]. The 
authors emphasized that this improvement was due to the 
ability of Pilates to increase core stability and strengthen the 
lower extremity [32]. In our study, all balance tests showed 
improvement, with a greater improvement in static balance 
tests. So our results are parallel to literature in improving 
balance. We think that our results are related to the improved 
deep abdominal muscle strength responsible for the stabili-
zation of the core area.
The outcome measurements used in our study focus on 
impairments of the patient, but did not include assessment 
of activities of daily living and participation of the patient. 
Future studies with inclusion of detailed evaluation of these 
components are suggested.
Conclusion
Physiotherapy-based clinical Pilates training provided 
improvements in ROM, flexibility, strength, functional 
mobility and balance measurements and also decreased pain 
level in the patient with SPS, and may offer an effective 
and safe intervention method. Although we have promis-
ing results, we cannot generalize these results to the disease 
population. More replication of research with bigger samples 
are needed to draw certain conclusions and to increase the 
level of evidence.

segments.text:
The aim of the present report is to show the effects of a clinical pilates-based physiotherapy training program on physical 
functioning, including balance ability, flexibility, muscle strength, and pain severity in a case with Stiff Person Syndrome 
(SPS). A 43-year-old female with a 3-year history of SPS participated in the study. Clinical pilates training exercises were 
performed two times per week during 8 weeks. Static balance was evaluated with One Leg Stance Test and Tandem Stance 
Test, dynamic balance with Functional Reach Test and lower extremity strength and endurance measured by 30-s Chair Stand 
Test. Berg Balance Scale was used to assess balance and fall risk, and Timed Up and Go Test was used to assess functional 
mobility. Pain evaluation was done by Pain Quality Assessment Scale. Flexibility was measured with tape measure, range 
of motion with goniometer and muscle strength with manual muscle test. Among the balance and functional mobility tests, 
progress has been observed in all tests, except for 30-s Chair Stand test. Improvements have been observed in patient’s range 
of motion, flexibility, strength, pain and balance parameters. Clinical pilates-based physiotherapy program had positive 
effects on many physical and functional parameters of the patient and can be used as a safe exercise method in physiotherapy 
rehabilitation of SPS.

segments.text:
Case presentation
AE is a 43-year-old women (BMI: 22.9 kg/m2) who referred 
to physiotherapy center for evaluation and treatment of low
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
back pain and gait disturbances associated with SPS. Her 
diagnosis had been confirmed by a neurologist at a major 
state hospital. Patient is an assistant manager at a bank and 
thinks her job is stressful and she has quite a lot of respon-
sibility. She is married and has two children. She has no 
known other illness than SPS.
Disease history
The patient first applied to a neurologist with numbness and 
tingling in lower and upper extremities, as well as neck and 
low back pain and fatigue at the beginning of 2016 and diag-
nosed as Parkinson’s Disease (PD). Over time, the patient 
complained about muscle stiffness increasing gradually 
until night. She stated that she has increased difficulty in 
walking, increased muscle spasms and PD drugs did not 
work. Also, the patient had started to experience recurrent 
falls which affected her daily activities. At the beginning of 
2017, she had been re-examined thoroughly by her neurolo-
gist with blood tests, X-ray, magnetic resonance imaging 
and computed tomography scan, and high serum level of 
GAD antibodies confirmed that she has SPS. The patient 
firstly applied to a physiotherapy and rehabilitation clinic 
in a medical institution with complaints of stiffness, pain, 
balance disorder and functional limitations. However, she 
stopped treatment by saying that her mobility was not getting 
better and her motivation lost. Her doctor recommended the 
patient to try Pilates training and she started Pilates training 
for 1 year, 3 sessions per week with a personal trainer. This 
training improved her pain level, but her spasms did not 
decrease and her stiffness continued. After three months of 
ending this training, her neurologist referred her to join a CP 
training program conducted by a certified physiotherapist in 
this area. The symptoms and complaints of the patient made 
her physician and physiotherapist to think that this train-
ing method can improve physical and functional capacity of 
the patient which is shown to be effective in these types of 
physical impairments and functional limitations in patients 
with neurologic problems.
When the patient applied for CP training, she had com-
plaints about increased low back pain, balance distributions 
during the day and frequent spasms toward the end of the 
day. She also indicated that she has difficulties in leaning 
forward and wearing shoes. On examination, she showed 
signs of rigidity in lumbar region as well as in lower and
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
upper extremities. She had no tremor and was having trouble 
lying on bed and turning around in bed. Her medications at 
the time of evaluation include gabapentin, benzodiazepine 
and weekly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg).
Before the study, the patient was informed in detail 
about the study protocol and the informed consent form 
was signed. Medical treatment of the individual continued 
in the same way. No changes were made in the drugs recom-
mended by the neurologist during the study. The case has 
been evaluated in detail at the beginning and end of the study 
by the primary investigator (BBK).
Physiotherapy evaluation
Range of motion
Goniometric measurements were made for joints of upper 
extremity, lower extremity and vertebral column. Range of 
motion (ROM) values of the patient’s back extension, all 
movements of the hip, knee flexion–extension, ankle dorsi-
plantar flexion, all movements of the shoulder and elbow 
flexion–extension were evaluated [19].
Flexibility
Flexibility was measured with the method suggested by 
Karaduman [20]. Trunk hyperextension, trunk lateral flex-
ion, hip abduction movement flexibility and hamstring and 
quadriceps femoris muscle flexibility were measured.
Muscle strength
For muscle strength testing, manual muscle testing method 
was used. 0–5 measurements were made using standard tech-
niques described by Clarkson and Gilewich. The strength of 
patient’s lumbar extension, all movements of the shoulder, 
elbow flexion and extension, all movements of the hip, knee 
extension–flexion, ankle dorsiflexion–plantar flexion move-
ments were measured [19].
Pain
Pain severity was measured by Pain Quality Assessment 
Scale (PQAS). The PQAS asks respondents to rate the 
severity of each of 20 pain (quality and spatial) descriptor 
domains using 0–10 numeric rating scales, in which 0 indi-
cates “no pain” and 10 “the most pain sensation imagina-
ble.” With this scale, the severity of the pain was determined 
according to the type [21].
Balance
Static balance of the participants was measured by One Leg 
Stance Test (OLS) [22] and Tandem Stance Test (TST) [23] 
which are valid methods to measure the ability to balance 
and stand. These tests also gives an idea about the balance 
ability of the individual and the risk of falling. Dynamic 
balance was tested by Functional Reach Test (FRT) which 
is a reliable and valid measure [24]. The patient is asked to 
lift his arm 90° up and place it at shoulder level and to lean 
forward as far as he can on the edge of the wall without 
any loss of movement or balance in the feet. The reduced 
reach ability indicates an increased risk of falling. 30-s Chair 
Stand Test which is a reliable and valid measure used to 
assess lower extremity strength and endurance. The number 
of sitting and getting up within 30 s gives the score of the 
test [25]. Risk of falling together with static and dynamic 
balance performance was measured by Berg Balance Scale 
(BBS) which is a commonly used, reliable and valid meas-
ure. It is a 14-item test that uses sequential scoring from 0 to 
4 for each item. The total score range is between 0 and 56, 
and a higher score indicates a better balance [26].
Functional mobility
Functional mobility was evaluated with the Timed Up and 
Go Test (TUG) which is a reliable and valid test. When the 
command "Go" is given, the patient stands up from a normal
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
chair, walks 3 m, turns and walks back to the chair and sits. 
Time begins when commanded and ends when the person 
sits back in the chair [27].
Intervention
CP-based physiotherapy training was performed twice a 
week during 8 weeks with a certified physiotherapist (FC) 
who was blinded to assessment results. The movements of 
main exercises implemented within the scope of CP train-
ing included: Warm-up exercises (15 min): Posture exer -
cises*, Calisthenic exercises*, ROM*, Upper Extremity 
PNF patterns, Mini Squat, Spine Stretch*, Chest Stretch*. 
Main exercises (30 min): Standing balance exercises, block 
jumping, side walking, cross walking, tandem walking. Mat 
exercises: Hundreds, Shoulder Bridge, One leg stretch, Hip 
twist, Oblique Preparation, Abdominal preparation, Arm 
openings, Side Kick, Lift lower, Left Lifts, Clam Prone posi-
tion; Swan dive, One leg kick, Swimming, Cobra. Cool-
down exercises (15 min): Cat Stretch*, Spine Stretch, The 
Saw, Mermaid, Chest stretch, Swinging, Quadriceps femo-
ris stretching*, Gluteus maximus stretching*, Hamstring 
stretching*, Hip flexor stretching* and end of the cool-down 
exercise, relaxation training* is applied such as: positioning
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
supine, supported by pillows. Along with positioning, res-
piratory control consisted of breathing exercises. In addition, 
a home program was given to the patient, which consisted 
of * exercises, to do 1 h per day (for the days when she does 
not join to program) and it has been checked every session.
Results
Table  1 shows the results of balance and functional mobility 
tests and flexibility measurements. Among the balance and 
functional mobility tests, progress has been observed in all 
tests, except for 30-s Chair Stand test. In addition, improve-
ments were seen in all of the flexibility measurements.
Manual muscle test and ROM measurements are shown 
in Table  2. According to manual muscle testing, all muscle 
strength scores improved, except ankle dorsiflexion, shoul-
der internal–external rotation and elbow extension scores, 
bilaterally. In addition, according to ROM measurements, all 
ranges increased except hip flexion of the left side, adduc-
tion of the both side, internal rotation of the right side, ankle 
dorsiflexion of the left and shoulder abduction of the right 
side values.
Table  3 shows comparison of PQAS before and after 
treatment. It was observed that the total score of the scale 
decreased from 120 to 89. Especially in 10 items, there was 
an improvement: pain intensity, stinging pain, burning, 
crushing sensation, striking-type pain, numbness, tingling, 
spasm, spreading and feeling of heaviness. The biggest dif-
ference after treatment was seen in the spasm subscale. The 
patient stated the spasm score as 9/10 before the treatment, 
and 5/10 after the treatment. Apart from this, there was an 
improvement in stinging and burning pain. While the patient 
gave 9/10 for the sinking and burning-type pain points before 
the treatment, it was reported as 6/10 after the treatment.

segments.text:
Conclusion
Physiotherapy-based clinical Pilates training provided 
improvements in ROM, flexibility, strength, functional 
mobility and balance measurements and also decreased pain 
level in the patient with SPS, and may offer an effective 
and safe intervention method.
